about: A fixed retrieval test set: memories with known answers to a fixed list of questions.
All projects, people and events here are invented.
Each question lists the indexes (0-based) of the memories that answer it.
Questions marked paraphrase use different words than their answer, so word search alone cannot find them.

memories.content: Picked Postgres over MySQL for the orchard order store. We need row-level locking for stock counts and the team already runs Postgres for two other services. MySQL was rejected because nobody here has run it in production.
Stock counts are decremented inside the same transaction that creates the order line. A separate reserve step was tried first and left ghost reservations whenever the client dropped mid-flow.

The nightly reindex on the orders table caused a four minute outage because it ran with a full table lock. Cause: the index was rebuilt with plain REINDEX instead of CONCURRENTLY. Always use the concurrent form on live tables.

tags.name: outage
tags.description: incidents that took a service down

memories.content: The owner wants order ids shown to customers as short base32 strings, never raw integers. Sequential numbers leak how many orders exist.
Order export runs as a cron job at 02:00 and writes one CSV per warehouse to the shared bucket. Files older than 30 days are pruned by the same job.
Prices are stored as integer cents in a BIGINT column, not as floats or NUMERIC. Floats round wrong and NUMERIC made the reporting queries twice as slow in our benchmark.

tags.name: money
tags.description: how amounts are stored and shown

memories.content: A refund was issued twice because the webhook from the payment provider was delivered twice and the handler was not idempotent. Fix: store the provider event id in a unique column and ignore repeats.
Keep API error bodies in the shape {error: {code, message}}. The owner rejected free-form strings because the mobile client parses the code field.

Lantern renders the log view with a virtual list that only draws the visible rows. Drawing every line made the browser freeze on files over 50 MB. A paged view was rejected because people scroll through logs, they do not page.

Timestamps in mixed time zones made the merged view sort wrong. Cause: two agents wrote local time without an offset. Now every log line is normalised to UTC when it is parsed, and lines without a zone are assumed UTC and flagged.
Command-line flags use kebab-case and every flag has a one-line help string. Short forms only for the five most common flags; the owner found a cluttered help screen hard to read.
The colour theme is read from the theme.toml file in the user config folder. If the file is missing the built-in dark theme is used and no warning is printed.

Search inside a log file uses a plain substring scan with a small in-memory index of line offsets, not a full regex engine on every keystroke. Regex on each keystroke was rejected as too slow on large files; a regex mode is available behind a toggle.
Reading a log file that is still being written to returned half lines. Cause: the reader treated end-of-file as end-of-line. Now a trailing partial line is held back until a newline arrives.
Lantern is shipped as a single static binary with no runtime dependencies. Users install it on servers where they cannot add packages; a Python distribution was rejected for that reason.

Pipeline jobs are idempotent and keyed by the day they process. Re-running a day replaces that day's output rather than appending. This was chosen so a failed night can be re-run without a cleanup step.
The daily aggregate was off by one day for a week after the clocks changed. Cause: the job used local midnight to cut the day. Days are now cut at UTC midnight and the report labels say so.
Raw input files land in the inbox bucket under year/month/day prefixes. The loader picks up anything under yesterday's prefix and ignores files whose name does not end in .jsonl.
Do not add a new pipeline stage without a sample input file checked in next to it. The owner wants every stage runnable on its own from a fixture.

The scheduler stays a plain cron entry rather than a workflow engine. There are four jobs with a fixed order; a workflow engine would add a service to run and watch for very little gain. Revisit if the job count passes ten.

tags.name: tooling
tags.description: tools we chose or turned down

memories.content: Out-of-memory crashes on the join stage came from loading both sides fully. The fix was to sort both inputs by key and stream them as a merge join; memory use went from 12 GB to under 1 GB.
Job output goes to the warehouse table daily_metrics. Each row carries the pipeline version that produced it so bad runs can be found and dropped later.
Secrets for the pipeline are read from environment variables set by the runner, never from a file in the repo. A checked-in encrypted file was rejected because rotating a key would need a commit.
Push notifications are queued in a table and sent by a worker, not sent inline from the request handler. Inline sending made request latency depend on the push provider, which was slow at peak.

Users got the same notification three times after a worker restart. Cause: the worker marked rows as sent only after the provider call, and a crash between the two left rows unmarked. Now the row is claimed with a lease before the call.
Notification text is at most 120 characters and never contains the user's name. The owner wants messages readable on a lock screen and safe if someone else sees the phone.
Device tokens that the provider reports as invalid are deleted right away. A cleanup job also drops tokens not seen for 90 days.

Rate limiting is per user per hour, enforced in the worker rather than at the API edge. Edge limiting was rejected because one user can trigger a burst from many endpoints and only the worker sees the total.

Login sessions expired at the wrong time on devices with a wrong clock. Cause: expiry was compared against device time. The server now returns a time-to-live in seconds and the client counts down from receipt.
The kestrel backend logs in JSON, one object per line, with a request id on every line. Plain text logs were dropped because following a request across the worker and the API was too slow by hand.
